data.title: New bill would restrict SNAP benefits in 9 states. Here's what could be cut
data.description:
Related video above: SNAP error rates could change benefits

(NEXSTAR) – A new law introduced in the House this month would add more restrictions to what types of food SNAP recipients can buy with their monthly benefits.

The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) helps about 37 million Americans buy food, mostly in the form of groceries. But in nine states, some SNAP beneficiaries who have a hard time preparing fresh food for themselves can also use their EBT cards to buy hot meals from approved restaurants.

A new bill, introduced by Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas), would eliminate that option.

The bill would eliminate SNAP’s Restaurant Meals Program (RMP), which states can opt in to. The program is meant to help people who can’t easily cook, or don’t have permanent housing, get access to food.

California, one of the select states where the Restaurant Meals Program is currently operating, says RMP targets “people that are a high risk for chronic hunger,” like those with disabilities or the homeless.

Not everyone can sign up for RMP and not every restaurant is an approved vendor. In order to qualify, SNAP recipients must be either elderly, disabled, homeless or the spouse of an RMP participant.

Only nine states have currently operating Restaurant Meals Programs, according to the USDA: Arizona, California, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, New York, Rhode Island and Virginia.

The bill, titled “Ending Restaurant Purchases with SNAP Act of 2026,” would amend federal law to cut the program entirely. Rep. Gill described RMP as a “loophole” that allows federal benefits to be spent on unhealthy food.

“SNAP is supposed to help struggling Americans put nutritious food on the table, not stick taxpayers with the bill for fast food,” Rep. Gill said in a statement to Newsweek. “More than half a billion dollars in SNAP benefits have gone to restaurants through this loophole in just two years while the Trump administration is working to get junk food out of the program. My bill ends this ridiculous loophole and makes sure SNAP dollars are used for what the program was created to do: help Americans afford nutritious groceries.”

The second Trump administration has placed increasing focus on what types of food SNAP dollars can and can’t purchase as part of its push to “Make America Healthy Again.” Twenty-three states had been granted waivers to bar SNAP recipients from spending the federal dollars on things like soda, energy drinks and candy before a judge struck down the new restrictions in June.

Critics say the added restrictions unnecessarily stigmatizes the food choices of low-income Americans.

“It’s an opportunity to say you’re doing something, while really just stigmatizing a single group of people for choices that everybody in America really makes,” Chris Bernard of Hunger Free Oklahoma told Nexstar’s KFOR.

A different approach has been proposed in the “Fresh Bucks for Fresh Produce” Act, introduced in Congress in July. The legislation would establish a pilot program granting households an extra $60 a month that could only be spent on fruit or vegetables.

Both bills have been referred to the House Committee on Agriculture for consideration.

data.title: The dangerous evolution of Gavin Newsom
data.description:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) wants you to know that he is evolving.

Newsom is facing a rising radical movement among Democrats, including a surging contingent aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America. He is struggling in polls and therefore eager to show the skill identified by Darwin that allows certain species to thrive in their environment: adaptation.

Newsom has recently declared capitalism a failure. He is now joining his competitors for president in offering up the Supreme Court and its independence to the far left. His free fall into rage politics is a cautionary tale for those who want to return the Democratic Party to more centrist positions.

Often called a “political chameleon,” Newsom seems to be morphing into the actual species that evolved to adjust to its environment, including more nimble feet.

Although natural selection takes place over many years and even eons, Newsom does not have the luxury of time. He does not want to be eliminated by the more politically fit opponents to his left.

Polls continue to show he receives more media support than public support. He trails Kamala Harris by 15 points in recent polling and is nearly tied with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.

Harris and Buttigieg quickly turned their backs on the norms governing the Supreme Court to support court-packing. Harris dismissed those of us in opposition as engaging in mere “nostalgia.” 

Newsom had previously tried to offer a sane alternative to these voices. But he has now found himself their quiet companion in a primal scream session. As he began to vanish in political polling, he decided he would not be outcrazied by Democratic opponents. 

With candidates like Texas’s Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico calling for the “dismantling” of capitalism as an “oppressive system,” Newsom finds himself needing to cater to the mob. He has now declared that “nostalgia is not working” while adding that “capitalism as we know it doesn’t work either.”

Newsom has recently been campaigning in blue states such as New Hampshire, repeating his mantra that capitalism as “not working.”

But these days, it is not enough for socialists and the far left merely to oppose the most successful economic system in the history of the world. Newsom was still being labeled as an establishment politician. So he tried to dispel that impression with his signature toothy grin and astonished demeanor, claiming that he is really undermining the system from within as “an established insurgent.”

Again, that is not enough for the current political environment. So this week, he changed his position on the Supreme Court, to say that he is now “open” to court-packing.

Packing the court is considered essential today for any viable Democratic candidate. Some are openly calling for the imposition of a litmus test for all candidates: As they put it, it is a choice between “packed or sacked.”

Even moderate figures such as Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) have now yielded to the mob in expressing a willingness to pack the Supreme Court.

So Newsom wants the far left to know that he is yet again evolving: “My initial instinct — me, a year ago, I would have said no out of concern that it will continue to be expanded. … I’m finding myself evolving on it.”

The question is what Newsom and his Democrat opponents will offer next in their political adaptation. These candidates have shown that no institution or value is more important than their securing power. At this rate, we will be fortunate to have anything more than the ship itself after the race to toss institutions and “nostalgic” values over the side.

The danger for Newsom — like the danger of any fast-tracking of evolution — is that the environment can change, leaving you with an adaptation that makes you even more likely to be eliminated. Newsom knows that attacking our constitutional or economic systems will not play well in the general election, but he also knows he will never see the 2028 general election if his opponents on the left outflank him.

Moreover, offerings like the Supreme Court or our economic system are unlikely to satiate the far left. As I discuss in “Rage and the Republic,” history shows that establishment figures rarely survive the mob politics they seek to use for their own advantage.

In the meantime, because of the cynical calculations of leaders like Newsom, we face a growing threat of doing lasting harm to our constitutional system. The framers warned us of these voices of “mobocracy” that would tear apart the contemporary revolution in France, which became known as “the Terror.”

The danger is that, while the majority opposes court packing and socialism, the new majority in Congress could force changes without amending the Constitution. That certainly can be done with court packing. Once a new liberal majority is secured, there would then be little barrier to achieving many of the objectives of a radical agenda long discussed by professors and pundits. Some have argued that, with control of the court and radical constitutional changes, Republicans will not be able to win another election.

In other words, the radicals hope to change the environment to prevent further adaptation and future competition.

Kurt Vonnegut once said, “Evolution can go to hell as far as I am concerned. What a mistake we are.” After watching the chameleonic Gavin Newsom, it seems that we may be on the cusp of precisely such an evolutionary mistake.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the New York Times best-selling author of “Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution.“

data.title: Live updates: Trump visits Ireland, the debate over 5K dividends heats up
data.description:
President Trump’s pledge to give $5,000 to every U.S. adult if Republicans keep control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections has raised questions over whether the plan could cross legal lines.  

Trump announced the dividends on the first night of the Republican National Committee (RNC) midterm convention in Dallas Wednesday night.

Those on the right and left has expressed their concerns on how Trump’s dividends would work, given the federal government would have to send out an estimated $1.2 trillion, according to The Hill’s Sophie Brams.

South Carolina Rep. Ralph Norman (R) was among those in the GOP to speak out against the idea, saying on the social platform X he had “serious concerns” about the plan.

With the midterm elections less than two months away, Trump will head to battleground North Carolina to campaign with GOP Senate nominee Michael Whatley on Wednesday.

Unlike Whatley, other candidates are choosing to keep Trump at an arm’s length, according to The Hill’s Julia Manchester.

Trump is in Ireland this weekend and met with Irish President Catherine Connolly and Taoiseach Micheál Martin.

Follow live below.

data.title: Trump says a unified Ireland is 'going to happen eventually'
data.description:
President Trump waded into hot water on Saturday when he expressed optimism about the reunification of Ireland during a meeting with Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin in Dublin. 

The president, who is visiting his Irish golf course this weekend for a major golf tournament, said he would “love” to see the joining of the Republic of Ireland and the U.K.’s Northern Ireland. 

“I’d love to see it unified,” Trump said. “I think that’d be a great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. It’s going to happen eventually.”

He pointed to Martin, adding, “You’ve got the right man over here to get it moving.”

The president noted that “the U.K. will have something to say about it, obviously.”

Previous U.S. presidents have typically avoided directly commenting on this contentious issue. Ireland’s split followed decades of violent conflict, called “the Troubles,” in Northern Ireland over whether to unite with the rest of Ireland or to remain part of the U.K.

The Good Friday Agreement, which the U.S. helped broker to end this conflict, gives the secretary of Northern Ireland the ability to call a border poll if it seems likely that a majority of people in the region would support Irish unification. 

On Wednesday, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham told British parliament members that he was “not aware that there is majority support for another referendum.”

“Until that changes, there will not be one,” he added.

Kemi Badenoch, the leader of the U.K.’s Conservative Party, slammed Trump’s comments in a social media post on Saturday. 

“President Trump is shooting from the hip as usual, just like he did with Greenland and Canada becoming the 51st state,” she wrote. “This sort of loose talk about the future of democratic countries is deeply unhelpful and creates unnecessary tension. 

“Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom,” Badenoch continued. “At a time when separatists are in power in Scotland, Wales and NI, we need a Government that will defend the Union clearly and confidently.”

Gavin Robinson, the leader of the U.K.’s Democratic Unionist Party who represents Northern Ireland in Parliament, also reacted to the president’s comment in a social media post. 

“President Trump knows better than most that elections matter,” Robinson said. “Northern Ireland’s constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington.”

Robinson expressed his confidence that the people of Northern Ireland “will continue to choose the UK and the security it offers.”

data.title: For many Democrats this cycle, the tipping point between victory and defeat is Israel
data.description:
Beneath their putative big tent, the national Democratic Party is embroiled in an ideological civil war that is likely to intensify through the 2028 presidential campaign. 

While there are many topic Democrats disagree on — socialism, transgender issues, open borders and appeals to the white working class — the one that underlies this battle for the party’s soul is U.S. support for Israel.  

“The genocide in Gaza has had an overwhelming effect on large, significant segments of the American public,” said Ian Lustick, co-author of the new book, “Israel’s Lobby: America in the Grip of a Foreign Power.“ “Israel’s policies in the past 20 years have become essentially indefensible.”

For Jews critical of the Netanyahu regime, the horrific Oct. 7 Hamas attack (1,200 Israelis killed; hundreds taken hostage) did not justify killing thousands of Gaza civilians or targeting journalists and emergency medical personal with supposedly precision air strikes. 

For single-issue, pro-Likud Jews, having a Democratic Party united against further U.S. aid to Israel means they would rather have a JD Vance or Marco Rubio in the White House, and a Republican-controlled Congress.

In U.S. Senate races in Michigan and Georgia, pro-Likud activists are supporting Republican campaigns. 

Shocked by Abdul El-Sayed’s Democratic primary victory, prominent Detroit businessman Eric Bronstein — a Democrat — wrote an open letter to Jewish Democrats and independents in support of Republican Senate candidate and former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.). Several Jewish Democratic bundlers later met for a Rogers fundraiser.

Other Michigan Jewish Democrats, like Attorney General Dana Nessel, disagree, declining to endorse Rogers. “We have a moral imperative to place the needs of the world above even our own self-interest and, yes, even our own survival,” she told a gathering of Jewish Democrats, provoking Likud supporters’ outrage.

In Georgia, in an open letter to Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) — Jewish, up for reelection and a possible 2028 presidential aspirant — Atlanta Jewish Times publisher Michael Morris called on Ossoff to “stop lying to me and your constituents” about his “ironclad support for Israel. … Your antagonism toward Israel has remained steadfast.”

El-Sayed and Ossoff recently rejected controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker’s alleged antisemitic postings. That was insufficient and too late, legacy Jewish organizations said.

In Florida’s U.S. Senate primary, state Rep. Angie Nixon (D), a democratic socialist, has repeatedly accused Israel of committing genocide. She criticized the favorite for the nomination, Alex Vindman, for silence on Israel. She introduced a bill in the Florida legislature calling for a “de-escalation and ceasefire in the state of Israel and occupied Palestine,” supports cutting U.S. aid for the Jewish state and refuses AIPAC money. Nixon’s position on military aid to Israel helped her upset win.

Across the country, accepting AIPAC money has proved toxic for many congressional candidates. For decades, AIPAC threw its weight (and money) around with supplicants. But in insurgent primary campaigns this year, accepting AIPAC-sourced campaign money has become a liability. 

Rogers’s campaign in Michigan is nervous, asking AIPAC to lie low and routing the cash from its superPAC, United Democracy Project, to a separate non-campaign group. Notwithstanding, Jewish Insider reports that Rogers attended four AIPAC fundraisers in Los Angeles over a long weekend in late August.

Even in deep-red Oklahoma, one candidate in the Senate Democratic primary ran a social media spot featuring a giant red bin labeled “AIPAC Funds,” with a caption reading, “Just taking out the trash.” The candidate, N’kiyla Jasmine Thomas, trounced her pro-Israel opponent, centrist Jim Priest.

Of course, there are still some imponderable “ifs” ahead. If, for example, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is turned out of office in October, that may affect U.S. Israel supporters’ internal debates.

Ironically, approaching the fall midterms, Democrats are much less divided than current struggles over Israel would suggest. From the center-left Democratic governors of swing states who support Israel, like Pennsylvania’s Josh Shapiro, to progressives like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York City, consensus exists on November’s campaign agenda: economics, affordability, Medicare for All, higher federal minimum wage, free preschool and no AI data centers.

I have a modest proposal for Democrats: Put off this searing fratricidal controversy over Israel until after the midterms. Don’t fight over the spoils of victory until there is a victory to fight over.

Mark I. Pinsky is a journalist and author based in Durham, N.C. He was a civilian volunteer attached to the IDF in El Arish, Sinai, in the summer of 1967.

data.title: Trump says he would allow Chinese automakers to build cars in US
data.description:
President Trump said Friday he would permit Chinese automakers to move manufacturing to the U.S. over the protest of American automakers. 

“If China wanted to come in and open a plant to build their cars here, I’d be OK with it,” the president told Fox News’s Laura Ingraham on “The Ingraham Angle.” 

“Japan does it, but they hire our people,” he continued. “The big thing is they hire our people.”

The president’s comment comes ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington, D.C., in two weeks. The Chinese leader is expected to bring a large business delegation with him during this visit, Reuters reported. 

Trump touted his “very good relationship” with Jinping ahead of this bilateral summit, telling Ingraham the meeting will “be interesting.”

“People say, ‘Oh, he spies on us.’ Well, we spy on him too,” the president said. “We’re very good at it also, so we get along.”

Former President Biden imposed a regulation in 2025 that effectively bans Chinese automakers from selling or manufacturing passenger vehicles in the U.S. Additionally, the U.S. has over 100 percent tariffs in place on Chinese electric vehicles.

Last week, the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, a trade organization representing all major American automakers, asked congressional leaders in a letter to place a “permanent ban” on Chinese-made cars in the U.S. 

“Enacting a permanent ban on Chinese vehicles and high-risk hardware and software in the 119th Congress will send a clear and bipartisan message that China’s strategy to dominate global automotive manufacturing will be met with a national security policy response from the American government,” wrote the group’s President and CEO John Bozzella. 

In July, the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee approved legislation that would ban companies from the U.S. market with over 15 percent Chinese ownership.

A similar House bill introduced earlier this year would bar the importation, manufacturing and sale of connected vehicles and vehicle software from a foreign adversary.

data.title: McConnell's return shines spotlight on older lawmakers
data.description:
Sen. Mitch McConnell’s (R-Ky.) expected return to the Senate next week is drawing attention again to the health of aging lawmakers.

McConnell, 84, was hospitalized over the summer for nearly two months after falling at home and receiving treatment for pneumonia. He has since been recovering at home and engaging in what he described as an “intensive regimen of physical therapy.” 

His extended absence and advanced age have reignited conversations about lawmakers staying in office too long, with polls showing many voters support term limits, even as they also keep reelecting elder statesmen.

McConnell was first elected to the Senate in 1985 and is the 10th longest-serving senator in U.S. history. He is not seeking reelection to his current term, which ends in January. 

Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D) has repeatedly raised questions over whether McConnell is fit to serve because of his health challenges this summer.

“I hope that he is one of the reasons that we get term limits. I’ll tell you what, I’d even name the bill after him,” he told CNN.

Iowa’s 44-year-old Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Rob Sand, has voiced his support for both age and term limits. 

“The idea is, I want term limits. I want age limits. Let’s go get them,” he told reporters in April.

Compounding these arguments is the recent spate of lawmakers who have died in office, six in this term alone. Reps. Raúl Grijalva (D-Ariz.) Gerry Connolly (D-Va.) and David Scott (D-Va.) were a decade or more past the typical retirement age of 65. Sen. Lindsay Graham (R-S.C.) was 71 when he died in office in July from aortic dissection a sudden condition that is not typically screened for.

In 2023, 90-year-old Sen. Dianne Feinstein (D-Calif.) died while in office.

Rep. Kay Granger (R-Texas) had left office just over a year before her death last month at age 83. The end of her tenure was marred by the revelation that she had been residing in a senior living facility and experiencing what her son Brandon Granger described at the time as “dementia issues.” Her family confirmed her death was caused by complications from Alzheimer’s disease. 

Support for term limits on Congress remains overwhelmingly popular among Americans across the political spectrum. 

An NPR/PBS News/Marist Poll released in May found that 83 percent of U.S. adults support term limits, with self-identified Republicans showing the highest rate of support at 89 percent. The same survey found that 80 percent of Americans also support an age cap on congressional candidates. 

According to Aaron Dukette, senior strategist for the nonpartisan advocacy group U.S. Term Limits, support for imposing term limits has “skyrocketed” among Congress members in the past few years. 

“We have 130-plus people who have signed a pledge and gotten on as co-sponsors for our amendment. So, it’s not obviously at the two-thirds threshold that you need to have both chambers, but it’s certainly growing,” Dukette told The Hill. “And I think people on both sides of the aisle started to recognize that this is something that’s going to benefit our whole electoral process and not just one party over the other.” 

The joint resolution supported by his organization proposes limiting U.S. senators to two terms and House members to three terms. The version introduced in the House last year has 115 co-sponsors, 107 of whom are Republicans. 

Although conversations and support for term limits and age limits persist among the general public, the discussions are rarer among lawmakers themselves, according to those who’ve worked with them. 

Rodney Whitlock, managing director of Cozen O’Connor Public Strategies, was health policy adviser to Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) until 2015. Grassley, 92, is now the oldest member of Congress and was among the oldest when Whitlock last worked for him more than a decade ago. Grassley ranks as the longest-serving U.S. senator currently in the chamber, exceeding McConnell’s tenure by four years. 

“It is not as common as one would think, unless the member starts to have issues,” Whitlock said when asked whether lawmakers and their staff talk about age.

He argued that the issue of an aging workforce is a broad one.

“Nobody should be looking at this going, ‘This is a unique problem to members of Congress.’ No, it’s not. It is societal. It is our issues with aging. All of these things are part of this conversation,” said Whitlock. He noted that during his time as a congressional staffer, views on aging lawmakers were more respectful, but the discussions have since become “overtly political.” 

While describing that Grassley sees public service as a “calling,” Whitlock said there are “certainly” lawmakers who stay in office simply because they have “grown so accustomed to the lifestyle.”

Discussions about American gerontocracy encompass all branches of government. President Trump, 80, is the oldest person to be sworn in as U.S. president; former President Biden became the oldest sitting president, leaving office at 82.

At the Supreme Court, five out of eight sitting justices are past age 65; Justice Clarence Thomas is the oldest at 78. 

Dukette from U.S. Term Limits said his organization is focused on limiting congressional service based on terms over age, reasoning that limiting terms would naturally resolve the age issue. 

“We understand the concern and the desire for age limits, given the fact that we have many prominent elderly members of Congress that are running into health troubles while still being in office and they go … missing for a time,” said Dukette. “If it wasn’t for the 20, 30, 40-year careers that put them in that place in the first place — most members that run for Congress don’t start doing so in their 60s or 70s. They do so in their 40s or even in their 50s, and then they’re there for decades of service.” 

When reached for comment on his condition and expected return, McConnell’s office referred to the senator’s last public statement released at the start of August, in which he said he would “continue my recovery at home” and “continue to engage with my staff and colleagues on important Senate business.” 

The Hill has reached out to Grassley’s office for comment.

data.title: The Memo: Trump's convention may struggle to turn tide for GOP
data.description:
President Trump basked in the approval of the MAGA base during this week’s Republican midterm convention in Dallas.

But the bigger question is whether the event made any difference to a political landscape that is seriously challenging for Republicans as Election Day looms less than eight weeks away.

The Hill’s data partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) on Friday gave Democrats a 68 percent probability of taking control of the House, with control of the Senate — once considered relatively safe for the GOP — a 50-50 split. Virtually no significant polling has been conducted since the Republican gathering, however.

By Friday, it was notable how swiftly the national news agenda was moving on from the GOP convention. Instead, commemorations marking the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, were the focus of attention.

The most significant news from the Dallas event was Trump’s pledge to send a $5,000 “dividend” to every adult American citizen if Republicans win the elections in November.

But there are massive questions around this — even beyond the charge that it is, in essence, adjacent to bribery.

First of all, Trump has a record of making comparable pledges of windfalls from tariffs and from savings ostensibly made by the Elon Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).

None of those promises has materialized. 

On Thursday evening, Trump lashed out angrily at a reporter — Rachel Scott of ABC News — when she began asking a question about his track record in this respect. The website The Bulwark, often a locus of Trump criticism, compiled several clips of his past pledges.

Even among some Republicans, reaction has been lukewarm at best. A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests Trump’s plan would cost roughly $1.3 trillion — and at a time when the national debt is already over $40 trillion and the global bond markets are getting antsy about the state of the federal government’s finances.

A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests Trump’s plan would cost roughly $1.3 trillion — and at a time when the national debt is already over $40 trillion and the global bond markets are getting antsy about the state of the federal government’s finances.

Vice President Vance notably did not mention the proposal during his keynote address on Thursday night, though he had defended it when asked during a Fox News interview the previous evening.

On the same network, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) said his opinion of the idea would depend “on how it’s structured,” and that he favored a tax refund for people who are employed. “I don’t think we should be paying people that are not working,” he said.

Other Republicans were even more equivocal. Rep. Pat Fallon (R-Texas), also speaking on Fox News, said “President Trump isn’t saying that if we win we’ll do this. He’s saying we’ll be in a position to do this.”

But Trump took to social media on Friday to insist it would happen. “When I say something, I mean it!” he claimed.

Republican pollster David Winston cautioned against reading too much into the way other GOP members reacted, given that it appears few had advance notice of the proposal Trump unveiled.

“Part of the reaction you are hearing is that people are unsure,” Winston asserted. “They’re not saying it’s good or bad. When something like that gets dropped on you, you want some time to think through it.”

But others took a harsher view — including some Trump-skeptical Republicans.

Rick Tyler, a veteran GOP strategist who is often critical of Trump, called the dividend proposal “a gimmick,” adding “they don’t mean it.”

“I struggle with the level of sophistication of people thinking, ‘I’m going to get $5,000 if I vote for the Republicans,” Tyler said.

The broader political question over the Republican convention concerns the wisdom of making Trump so central to the party’s strategy heading into November.

The fundamental problem is Trump is significantly unpopular in the nation at large.

The DDHQ polling average on Friday afternoon found the president’s job performance eliciting disapproval from 57 percent of Americans and approval from 40 percent. Data analyst Nate Silver has Trump performing a few points worse, with just 38 percent approval.

Trump, as usual, proclaims enormous confidence. “Pretend I’m on the ballot,” he has said several times.

Democrats, however, are more than happy for Trump to be front and center.

“If Republicans in swing districts want to appear with Donald Trump, let the chips fall where they may,” Democratic strategist Julie Roginsky told this column. 

“I understand they are trying to get as many MAGA voters as possible, but I think even those voters who will turn up for Trump will not, at this point, turn up for Republicans in a midterm election. So I just think aligning yourself with Trump is political suicide,” Roginsky added.

Tyler reached a similar conclusion, but from a different route. 

The GOP strategist contended that there are indeed some times when it makes sense for a party to nationalize a midterm election. 

He cited the success enjoyed by Republicans back in 1994, when their-whip Newt Gingrich (R-Ga.), unveiled a “Contract with America.”

But, Tyler added, “when you are the party in power and affordability is the number one issue and not getting better, it is not the time to nationalize the election. It’s the time to localize the election, and make the election about the opponent and what would happen if the opponent got elected.”

He contended that the event in Dallas “did precisely the opposite. It highlighted ‘we are the people in charge, we’re the ones you’re not happy with.’”

Some Republicans argue that, for all the coverage the convention created, it is substantive factors like the economy and the war in Iran that will ultimately determine the outcome of the midterms.

Winston, the pollster, argued that Republicans still have time to turn things around.

“The key moment would be when someone can walk into a grocery store and think, ‘’I am better able now to handle these prices,’” he said. “That could happen anytime up until Election Day. Somebody could walk into a grocery store on the last day of October and have that thought.”

As a hypothetical, that may be true. But Trump’s approval ratings on inflation are especially poor, and new data released on Friday showed the annualized inflation rate unchanged at 3.4 percent.

If things are going to change for Trump and the GOP, they need to do so soon — regardless of the claims made from the stage in Dallas.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

data.title: Trump pledges $5K checks if Republicans do well in the midterms. Can he legally do that?
data.description:
President Trump’s pledge to give $5,000 to every U.S. adult if Republicans keep control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections has raised questions over whether the plan could cross legal lines.  

The president announced the so-called “Trump dividends” on the first night of the Republican National Committee’s (RNC) midterm convention in Dallas this week, suggesting the country’s roughly 270 million adults should share in his administration’s “tremendous economic success.”  

“Very much like a successful company will do a cash distribution to its shareholders,” Trump said, caveating that the money “must be spent” only inside the country.  

It was not immediately clear how the plan would work. The federal government would have to dole out an estimated $1.2 trillion, and doing so would likely require an act of Congress.

“It’s not something that the president can unilaterally do,” said Paul Berman, a professor at George Washington University Law School.

Congress holds appropriating power, meaning the executive branch cannot spend public money on something unless the legislature has specifically set aside funds for that purpose.

That was the case with the $1,776 checks sent to roughly 1.45 million U.S. service members around Christmas last year. Those payments came in the form of a one-time housing supplement that was added to the president’s sweeping tax and spending law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill.

And while Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) has said he would introduce legislation to make the midterm dividends a reality, Trump insists he doesn’t need it.  

“I think they will do it if we needed it, but we think not,” Trump told CBS News when asked about the need for congressional approval. “The country is doing so well. We’ve taken in trillions of dollars in tariffs and other things.”

Tariffs have generated roughly $341 billion in net revenue since the start of 2025, according to Treasury Department data cited by the Bipartisan Policy Center. At the same time, the Trump administration has been ordered to refund roughly $166 billion of that after the Supreme Court struck down its sweeping global tariffs in February.  

“First of all, there isn’t enough tariff revenue to cover this,” Berman said. “Even if there were, that’s money that goes back to the public fisc, and then Congress is the one that has the power of the purse to allocate it.”  

“So it would be, I think, not plausible to think that the president could simply give out this money,” he added.  

Aside from the budgetary hurdles, there’s also a question of whether the dividends could amount to an unlawful quid pro quo.  

Trump’s promise hinges on the GOP’s electoral success, a condition critics were quick to argue constitutes bribery.  

“Nothing says confidence like trying to bribe people for votes,” Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Mass.) wrote Thursday on the social platform X.  

Those criticisms also came from the other side of the aisle, with Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) noting “serious concerns” about how the plan would be paid for, and former Rep. Bob Good (R-Va.) referring to it as a “socialist-vote buying scheme.”  

Federal law makes it illegal to offer and receive money or anything of value in exchange for voting or withholding a vote — what is typically understood as the classic form of bribery.  

But experts say whether a campaign incentive —like the one Trump is proposing — steps over that line can depend on who benefits from it.  

The Supreme Court held in a 1982 case involving a Kentucky county commissioner candidate who pledged to reduce his salary if elected that broad campaign promises are considered constitutionally protected speech.  

“A candidate’s promise to confer some ultimate benefit on the voter, qua taxpayer, citizen, or member of the general public, does not lie beyond the pale of First Amendment protection,” Justice William Brennan, Jr. wrote in the unanimous opinion.  

That ambiguity was the question facing state prosecutors tasked with determining whether billionaire Elon Musk had violated the law when he handed out two $1 million checks during a campaign rally in Wisconsin ahead of the state’s Supreme Court election last year.  

Musk initially announced the incentive on social media as a show of “appreciation” for those “taking the time to vote.” But he later backtracked, clarifying in a separate post that the money would go to “spokesmen” for a petition against so-called “activist judges.”  

Tim Gruenke, the Democratic district attorney in La Crosse County, Wis., ultimately decided not to pursue charges, saying he did not believe a jury was likely to convict Musk because “nobody was paid anything of value for voting or promising to vote.”  

The Tesla CEO was separately sued in state court by a political watchdog group and several voters who argued that the handout was a “brazen scheme” to entice voters to pick his preferred judicial candidate. That case is currently pending.  

Any prospective legal challenge to Trump’s divided plan would likely face roadblocks, as Berman says it would likely be difficult to prove standing in federal court.  

“I mean that would be the biggest issue: Who is it who’s harmed?” he said, noting that a Democratic candidate who lost their election could theoretically make the argument. He also said it would be hard for Congress to mount a challenge because individual members typically don’t have standing to sue.  

“With regard to people receiving the money, they would have a hard time showing that they are harmed because obviously they’re receiving money,” Berman added.

data.title: North Korea fires ballistic missiles after condemning military drill as threat
data.description:
North Korea launched ballistic missiles toward the sea Saturday, a day after the U.S., South Korea and Japan completed a trilateral military drill in response to North Korean nuclear threats.

The missiles were launched from the Wonsan area on North Korea’s eastern coast, according to South Korea’s military. Seoul said it was closely monitoring its neighbor and coordinating with the U.S. and Japan.

U.S. Pacific Command said the missiles did not pose an immediate threat to the U.S. or its allies.

“We are aware of the recent missile launch and are consulting closely with our allies and partners,” the command said in a statement. “Based on current assessments, this event does not pose an immediate threat to U.S. personnel or territory, or to our allies.”

The launches came after the three countries wrapped up Freedom Edge on Friday. The military exercise, which began Monday, focused on training to respond to North Korea’s nuclear missile capabilities.

North Korea had opposed the drills, and warned earlier this week that it could respond.

North Korean Defense Minister Kim Song Gi said Pyongyang was capable of taking “strong and reflective countermeasures from the standpoint of power.”

The exercise went ahead weeks after South Korean and U.S. militaries scaled back a separate annual exercise — their 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises.

President Trump ordered the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” the exercises, citing both his good relationship with North Korean Supreme Leader Kim Jung Un and South Korea’s refusal to join U.S. efforts against Iran.
